findings.title: `resume_item` reports every `OSError` as a report-write failure
findings.description: `resume_item` wraps the whole locked body in `except OSError as exc: return ResumeOutcome(ResumeExit.HALTED, f"cannot write the batch report: {exc}")`. Only one of the OSErrors that can reach that handler comes from a report write. `_resume_locked` also runs `state_manager.load` (`state.py` `path.read_text`), `load_pipeline` (`open(path)`), `evaluate_each_source` → `_review_flag` → `read_frontmatter` (`Path.read_text`), and `run_git` plumbing — any of which can raise `OSError` (EACCES on a runs dir, a vanished design file, a full disk during a state write). In those cases the operator is told "cannot write the batch report", which names a cause that was never established, and `ResumeExit.HALTED` folds a possibly-transient read failure into the same bucket as a mid-item git halt. The design's D12 row ("Report temp write or rename | OSError | logger.exception, then re-raised … ERROR with the path") is narrower than what this handler actually catches. Catch the report-write failure where it is raised (or catch a dedicated error from `BatchReport.write`) and let other OSErrors name their own failure.

findings.title: The per-item report rewrite is outside the guard the halt path uses
findings.description: `_finish_each_report` deliberately catches `OSError` on the halt path "so the halting fault is the one that propagates", but the new per-item write is not on that path: `await _write_each_report(report, runs_dir, final=False)` runs inside the `try` after `in_flight = None`, so an `OSError` there unwinds into the `finally`, which then calls `_finish_each_report(..., in_flight=None, halt=None, ...)` → `_write_each_report` again with no handler, re-raising from the `finally` and replacing the original exception. The observable outcome (an `OSError`) is the same class, so nothing is swallowed, but the design's D7 contract ("written after every item, not only at the end") is delivered by a write whose failure is not classified the way the halt write is. Consider routing the per-item write through the same catch-and-log policy, or moving it after `in_flight` is cleared only for the terminal item.

findings.title: `_write_atomic` leaves its temp file behind and duplicates `state.py`'s helper
findings.description: `tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(..., delete=False)` + `temp.replace(target)` has no cleanup on the failure path: if `handle.write` or `temp.replace` raises, the `.{name}.<random>` file stays in the runs directory, so a repeated ENOSPC or permission failure accumulates dotfiles beside the run state. `StateManager._write_atomic` (`state.py`) already implements the same write-then-rename with a deterministic `.tmp` suffix; two helpers now do the same thing two different ways. The rename is what makes the "previous report stays intact" claim true, so this is cosmetic, but a `finally: temp.unlink(missing_ok=True)` and reaching for the existing helper would keep one atomic-write idiom in the codebase.

findings.title: `pipeline_mutates` walks only `steps:`, so a `fan_out` inner step is never inspected
findings.description: `_step_mutates` recurses through `config["steps"]`, which is the key `loop` and `each` bodies use. `fan_out`'s nested step lives under `inner` (`_execute_fan_out_step` reads `resolved_config["inner"]`), and `dispatch`/`review`/`summary`/`gate` are not in `_MUTATING_STEP_TYPES`, so a mutating step reachable only through `fan_out.inner` would not cause `sq run` to take the project lock. No built-in pipeline nests an implement/phase step under `fan_out`, and `fan_out`'s own validation forbids nesting another `fan_out`, so the practical exposure today is nil — but the design states the executor "finds them by walking the definition, nested steps included", and that claim does not hold for the `inner` key. A one-line addition for the `inner` key would make the walk match the stated rule.

findings.title: A `report.json` with a missing `index`/`name` loads as the string `"None"`
findings.description: `from_json` builds `values` with `data.get(key)`, then coerces with `str(...)`: `index=str(values["index"])` and `name=str(values["name"])`. A truncated or hand-edited report missing those keys yields the literal record `"None"` instead of a `BatchReportLoadError`, whereas a missing `outcome` does fail (its `ItemOutcome(str(None))` raises `ValueError`, which `BatchReport.load` converts). The class's own contract is "It never guesses", and the rendered Markdown line for such a record reads `- None — …`. Treating an absent `index`/`name` as malformed (or defaulting to the same `#{position + 1}` form `from_item` uses) would keep the loader's failure story consistent.
